body.text: Advocates warn Canberra's comparatively high income is masking rental unaffordability
In short:
The latest Rental Affordability Index found the average Canberra household was spending 22.6 per cent of its income on rent.
The ACT has introduced regulations around rental increases and has seen an increase in housing stock.
But an expert warns the positive headline figures for the national capital "only tell half of the story".
Once considered one of Australia's most unaffordable cities for renters, Canberra is now out in front when it comes to rental affordability.

The latest Rental Affordability Index has found Canberra to have the most "acceptable" rental market of Australia's capital cities, with the average renting household spending 22.6 per cent of its income on rent.
It is a marked improvement for the nation's capital, which was considered the second most unaffordable city for renters back in 2022.
Perth currently holds the title of having the least affordable rental market, followed by Hobart and Sydney.
So why has Canberra's rental market improved while other cities have seen a decline?
Rental caps could be working

The study, by CGS Economics and Planning and National Shelter, measures rental affordability relative to household incomes, and found the ACT has the highest average rental household gross income at $142,658 per year.

SGS Economics principal Ellen Witte said comparatively high average incomes had kept pace with rent increases in Canberra, partly due to rent stabilisation measures introduced by the ACT government in 2019.
Rent increases in Canberra can only happen once a year with eight weeks' notice, and they are capped at 10 per cent above the increase in the Consumer Price Index.
"There are some guardrails now ... and so it's still possible as a landlord to increase your rents, but not in an excessive way,"
Ms Witte said.
The high incomes and targeted policy have helped buffer Canberra from declines seen in other jurisdictions like Hobart and Perth, Ms Witte said.
"Out of the seven capital cities in Australia, five are tracking very poorly — where even the average income household is now struggling to pay rent — and only two are getting better," she said.
"Canberra is getting better [and] Melbourne is stabilising, and it just happens to be so that those are the two jurisdictions that put in place some regulations around rent increases."
Unaffordable for low-income renters
While Canberra may be considered the most affordable city for renters overall, it remains unaffordable for low-income earners and students.
ACT Shelter chief executive Corinne Dobson said the positive headline figures "only tell half of the story", with Canberra's high average incomes masking a "two-tier" rental system.

"We do see really high rates of rental stress, and that's because the rental market is more pitched towards the average income and people on average incomes in the ACT are earning a lot more than elsewhere," she said.

"But if you're someone who's on a lower income, if you're on income support, or maybe you're in early childhood education and care or in hospitality, it is really tough finding an affordable rental in the ACT."
The study found people who worked in hospitality and rented in the ACT were spending an average of 38 per cent of their income on rent, while early childhood educators were spending 37 per cent.

A person on JobSeeker payments and rental assistance in Canberra sees 99 per cent of their income go to rent, while median rents were taking up 62 per cent of a single pensioner's aged pension income.
"For people on the lowest incomes, we do see the highest rates of rental stress here in Canberra, and that's been the case for well over a decade and it continues to be the case,"
Ms Dobson said.
For students, like Dylan Adams, Canberra's rental market has been proving incredibly difficult; he has been looking for a new place for months.

"The houses that are more affordable for students usually have one or two or many issues with them, whether it's mould in the bathrooms, or there aren't enough bathrooms, or the quality of the kitchen is poor," he said.
He is now considering a second job on top of his studies so he can afford to pay a higher rent.

"I'm looking at upping the amount of days that I work next year and potentially harming my studies to have enough money to rent a house that at least is a good enough quality that I feel like I can live in it properly,"
he said.
Low-income renters 'between a rock and a hard place'
Ms Witte said many tenants in Canberra were "between a rock and a hard place".
"What we see is parents skipping meals, at least then their children can eat; people skipping medicine, people turning homeless — even people with jobs are sometimes now living out of their cars,"
she said.
"Apart from financial hardship, there's a lot of social and psychological impacts.
"The fact that people can't participate in a whole range of activities anymore, children that can't participate in sports and things like that, is really affecting people's lives in so many ways."
That is something Mr Adams has experienced first-hand.

"Often it's a big joke for young people when they're renting houses to have two-minute noodle dinners every single night because their rent is so incredibly high that it's taking out a majority of their pay," he said.
